newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU treaty talks gain urgency on road to Amsterdam.
newsitem.headline: EU treaty talks gain urgency on road to Amsterdam.

text.p: While Europe's ambitious plan for a single currency lurches on through threats of fudge and delay, the 15-nation bloc will this week try to inject pace into gruelling talks aimed at re-shaping the Union for the new millennium.

The inter-governmental conference (IGC), overshadowed by the financial and political wrangling over economic and monetary union (EMU), approaches the final lap ahead of its expected completion at the Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.
Following 15 months of behind-the-scenes activity, the IGC will take centre-stage at a series of high-profile meetings in the Netherlands in the coming weeks.

EU foreign ministers gather in The Hague on Tuesday to review a draft treaty drawn up by the Dutch EU presidency and to prepare the ground for heads of government and state who meet in the coastal town of Noordwijk on Friday for an informal session to gauge the chances of a successful Amsterdam summit.

In addition, the bloc's Christian Democrat leaders, including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and the premiers of Ireland, Belgium and Luxembourg meet in Brussels on Wednesday to clarify a common position for Amsterdam.
The Noordwijk meeting will mark the EU debut of Tony Blair, whose crushing victory in British elections earlier this month has significantly increased the mood of optimism in Europe.

His more pro-European Labour government has signalled its intention to offer a constructive partnership in the Union in stark contrast to nearly two decades of negative Conservative tactics that so often left Britain isolated.
The IGC is designed to prepare for future enlargement that could boost bloc membership beyond two dozen within a decade.
Although the issues at stake are themselves relatively unspectacular, the overall package is aimed at making the bloc more efficient and open.
Months of detailed negotiation have resolved many areas, leaving a handful of more contentious issues to be thrashed out by EU leaders in these final, urgent bargaining rounds.

The new treaty's centrepiece will be the creation by 2002 of an area of freedom and security, lifting all internal borders except those around Britain and Ireland, and taking a firm stand against organised crime, drugs and illegal immigration.

Changes will also be made to the way the EU takes decisions, diluting the national veto by cutting back on the number of areas requiring unanimity and re-weighting the voting structure in favour of larger EU countries.
Job creation and the environment will be given a higher profile and some form of flexibility will be introduced to allow some countries to forge ahead and integrate faster than others.
Existing procedures for agreeing common foreign and judicial policies will also be strengthened. Foreign policy will be the main issue at Tuesday's meeting in the Hague.

While elections in France and Ireland in the weeks before the summit add an air of uncertainty, the demise of the British Conservatives was widely welcomed as having removed the biggest obstacle to an Amsterdam Treaty.
The former government was fiercely opposed to many of the issues favoured by its partners and had threatened to block the treaty if it failed to get its way in a number of areas.
Blair's "fresh start" has lifted that threat. His government has already embraced the social chapter and has pledged to cooperate in areas such as human rights and the environment.
But even Blair remains opposed to plans to integrate the Western European Union defence arm into the mainstream EU.
As the run-up to Amsterdam intensifies, few issues are as divisive as the number of seats each country should have on the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm.
